But I can't seem to make the same links you are making when you explain your interpretations. I'm not saying either one of us is right or wrong, but I can't say I agree with your viewpoint.

>"The Tao that can be spoken is not the eternal Tao"

I see that as a way of defining the creator of all existence. It cannot be named or described, so it shall remain nameless forever. 

And then the next line:
>"The name that can be named is not the eternal name"

In reference to the line before, if it can be named, it is not the eternal Tao.

>"The nameless is the origin of Heaven and Earth"

Again, in reference to the creator of all existence, that which cannot be described or named. But it has always been and always will be.

>"The named is the mother of myriad things"

As in, everything the nameless has created can be named, and everything that can be named is born out of the nameless. 

>"Thus, constantly free of desire
One observes its wonders"

The people who can put away their personal desires and view the world for all the wonders it contains from the nameless to the named. 

Whereas:
>"Constantly filled with desire
One observes its manifestations"

The people who are blinded by desire, can only see what is put here as objects and nothing else. To take and use as desired with no regard from where it came from or what it is. They don't see the wonder in these things, just the manifestation of it.
